title: Built an MMO with AI agents for 10 months. The real unlock wasn't codegen, it was writing everything down
author: Rough_Sheepherder386
selftext:
>Solo dev, browser hacking MMO, Go/Postgres/Redis/Svelte, live in production. Ten months, 7,816 commits, 1,385 merged PRs, one human. I'll skip the workflow diagram, other people have drawn better ones. Two things actually changed how I work, and one thing didn't change at all.  
>  
>The first is boring, which is how I know it's real: I made the agents read documentation. Not a context dump of source files. A small curated bundle, one page per game system, the architecture, conventions, a change log, kept true by a curator agent after every change. Early on, every session opened the same way, re-read half the codebase, re-derive the economy, misunderstand heat decay in some new confident way. Once the docs existed and were mandatory, the drift mostly stopped. What I didn't expect: writing those distillations improved my own design, because compressing a system to one page forces decisions the code was quietly fuzzing over.  
>  
>The second: specs and plans became the product. A design doc that says what we're NOT building is worth more than a week of generation. Most of what ships wrong ships wrong because the doc was wrong, and a wrong doc is the cheapest bug you'll ever fix, you edit text instead of five files.  
>  
>What didn't change: the game is still mine. Agents have no idea what's fun. They will happily build a perfectly specified boring mechanic, and the hour I spend spec-reviewing to catch that is worth more than everything else combined. A while back a race condition made three players swear their nodes had moved during a six-second glitch. They had moved. The agents found it fast. Knowing it mattered was me, reading the chat log at 1am.  
>  
>Numbers for anyone who wants them: 570 migrations, 551 test files, 880 commits with a Claude co-author line, one human reviewing all of it.  
>  
>If you're doing this, my whole experience compresses to one line: write down what you know, keep it current, make them read it. The generation was never the hard part.  
>  
>The game's free at [https://hiddenwars.io](https://hiddenwars.io) if you want to judge the output rather than the process.

comments.author: Outrageous-Issue9722
comments.body: Not discrediting the amount of work you put in, but I scrolled through your website and nothing at all looked like gameplay of any kind. I'd fix that, because it made me definitely not want to bother signing up or playing it.

replies.author: Rough_Sheepherder386
replies.body: Right, I did the Guest part for people to try but you are right nothing shows the game on the first page. I'm wondering what would be best, short GIF or videos showing some specific actions or screenshots only, what do you feel is more appealing ?

replies.author: Outrageous-Issue9722
replies.body: A trailer of some sort. Need something to get people curious.  Nothing on the current page made me curious.

comments.author: Fast-Sir6476
comments.body: I think it’s unfortunate that the first person to stumble on your post actually does cyber for a living. It’s a cool concept and probs cool for the avg gamer but I cringed too hard lol. Defs not for me

replies.author: Rough_Sheepherder386
replies.body:
Yes can't do realistic game about cyber, that would be too niche. Not many people have knowledge about it so it wouldn't work unfortunately.   
I'm actually adding some piece like a simulated shell where you have to solve puzzles, kind of CTF and you have the basic commands there but I feel it would still be hard on casuals

replies.author: Rough_Sheepherder386
replies.body: I introduce some concepts to players like encodings (I know it's basic) but still I feel it's cool to let them decode a ROT-13 > BASE64 to find the token during CTF events for example.

comments.author: SlopMachinez
comments.body: Document everything. I even have a daily journal with a summary of every interaction with my agents.

replies.author: Rough_Sheepherder386
replies.body: Interesting, I didn't think about keeping a journal of my interactions with the agents. I was more focus on distilling with Google's OKF the knowledge so the agents understand better the project as it goes and don't hallucinate or refer to things that is deprecated.

comments.author: Useful_Use_6170
comments.body: I joined as a guest and no onboarding, I didn’t know what I was doing obviously u do because you probably tested and fixed bugs

replies.author: Rough_Sheepherder386
replies.body: were you not greeted by S4B3R that tells you what to do at first ? Like your first hack and so on ?

replies.author: Rough_Sheepherder386
replies.body: thanks for the feedback and screenshot, I'm going to fix this asap

replies.author: Rough_Sheepherder386
replies.body: And it's a bigger topic, because I did different types of onboarding, and what I saw when really assisting players is that they don't read and just click next. So I thought an onboarding a bit more interactive with first missions and so on would be better.

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: Man I hate reading AI marketing posts talking about how many PRs someone made. Went to go to the site to see what its about and none of the videos actually played/loaded
